description:
The shrine of Hazrat Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari is one of the principal Sufi dargahs of the Jhal Magsi district of Balochistan, situated at Gandawah (Gandava), the historic administrative town of the Kachhi plain. Its saint bore the *Bukhari* lineage, marking descent from the influential family of Sayyids who traced their origins to Bukhara and whose forebears — most famously Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari of Uch Sharif — spread the *Suhrawardi* devotional tradition across Sindh and the southern Punjab. The tomb is locally admired as one of the finest examples of shrine architecture in the district, and it stands among a cluster of Sufi graves in the Gandawah area that together form an important sacred landscape for the surrounding Baloch and Brahui communities. Devotees from across the district and beyond visit to seek blessing and intercession, and the saint's *urs* is observed as the chief event of the devotional year, drawing pilgrims, *qawwali* and the distribution of food. As with many shrines of interior Balochistan, the documented history of the saint is thin and his dates uncertain, so his biography is best treated as living tradition rather than established record; the *Bukhari* attribution and the shrine's standing as a regional pilgrimage centre are, however, well attested locally. It should not be confused with the separate and larger Dargah of Fateh Pur Sharif (Pir Rakhail Shah), also in the Jhal Magsi district. Independent confirmation of the tomb's standing among Gandava's principal monuments comes from a 2019 Dawn survey of the town's heritage, which names "the tombs of Ayub Shah Bukhari, Murad Kaleri, and Meeri of Khan-e-Qalat" together with the Jamia Mosque of Gandava among "the best examples of Islamic architecture in the area," though the article gives no further individual detail — no dates or architectural description — specific to this tomb.

## Bibliography
- Sheikh Javed Ali Sindhi, "Heritage: A Refuge and Fort for Ancient Armies," *Dawn*, 22 December 2019.
qa_note:
This addition rests on a single independently-verified source (Dawn, 22 December 2019) confirming that a tomb of this name exists among Gandava's heritage sites; a second source that would likely corroborate this — the Jhal Magsi District Government's own heritage listing, reported by a sibling researcher's file to name "Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari (Gandawah)" among the district's main shrines via a Wayback Machine snapshot — could not be re-fetched this session and is not counted as verified here. This addition rests on a single independently-verified source and has not yet been corroborated.

Caution — possible same name, different site: English Wikipedia's uncitable "Ayub Shah Bukhari" article describes a distinctly-located shrine of this name in Gulshan-e-Maymar, Gadap Town, Karachi, associated with a January 2014 killing of six people (three shrine custodians, three others) claimed by the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan. None of the underlying sources for that Karachi claim (UCA News, an Indian Express archive page, the South Asia Terrorism Portal) could be independently fetched or verified this session, so it is not treated as a confirmed fact and has not been merged into this entry's description. It is flagged here only as an open question for a human to check: whether the "Hazrat Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari" of Balochistan described in this entry is the same figure as the "Ayub Shah Bukhari" of Karachi's Gadap Town, or an unrelated saint who happens to share the same Bukhari-sayyid honorific and given name.
